title: Like stars, like dew (section 32)
hook: look on the world like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud (Müller, section 32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, views of self: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Your line: so-called views.

Dew covers the car in the driveway at six in the morning, the windshield beaded and silver. By the time the coffee's poured, the sun is over the fence, and by the time the keys are found, the glass is dry. Nobody saw it leave. The Diamond Sutra has spent weeks cutting: self, marks, merit, views. Now, in its last section, it stops cutting and hands over a few pictures, plain enough for a child, and says: look at the world like this.
screen: `DEW ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `DRY BEFORE THE KEYS ARE FOUND.` → `THE BLADE HANDS OVER PICTURES.`

segments.voice: First, one last comparison. Someone fills worlds beyond measure with jewels and gives them all away. Someone else takes even four lines of this teaching, keeps them, and explains them to others. The second makes the greater merit. And how should it be explained? In the sutra's own way: without taking hold of the explaining, so that it's only called explaining. Then the verse. In paraphrase: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Each is something you can see. Stars shine all night and fade at dawn. A lamp burns only while the oil lasts. A magician's illusion. Dew, gone before the keys are found. A bubble. A dream that felt like a whole life. A flash of lightning. A cloud, changing shape as you watch. On day one hundred ninety-one, the Dhammapada asked you to look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage; here that same eye comes back. The verse doesn't say the world is fake. Dew is really dew; it really wets the glass. A few days ago the sutra warned against hearing emptiness as nothing. The verse holds both: real, and passing. Then the Buddha finishes, and Subhuti, the monks and nuns, the lay men and women, gods and humans and other beings all rejoice at what he has said. The Diamond Sutra began with an ordinary morning: a bowl, a meal, washed feet. It ends with a lamp, a bubble, and a crowd that is glad.
screen: `FOUR LINES OUTWEIGH THE JEWELS.` · `STARS, A LAMP, DEW, A BUBBLE.` · `REAL, AND PASSING.` · `THE ASSEMBLY REJOICES.` · then, large: `LIKE DEW, LIKE LIGHTNING.`

segments.voice: Watch something that forms and fades: bubbles rising in a fizzy glass, breath fogging a window, or, eyes closed, the breath itself as it forms, fills and goes. Let one picture from the verse sit with you, stars or dew or lightning. Notice the thing is real while it lasts, and that it doesn't last, and hold both gently.
Like stars. The first picture in the Diamond Sutra's closing verse: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Today's word.
Your line: like dew, like lightning. Real while it lasts, and then gone. The Diamond Sutra, done.

howItsDone: Some Mahayana communities recite the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra on its own, at the end of chanting the sutra and at other times, as a short reminder that all that is made is passing.

chat.says: That verse about dew and bubbles: is the Diamond Sutra saying life isn't real?
options: No. Dew really wets the glass; the verse says all that's made is real and passing, both.
Yes. It ends by saying the world is only a dream, so nothing that happens in it counts.
No. It means only the stars last forever, and everything below them passes away.
chat.meaning: The closing verse pictures all that's made as stars, dew, a bubble, lightning: real while it lasts, and passing, not fake.

Tathagata.meaning: the awakened one; a title the Buddha uses for himself

Subhuti.meaning: the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra

Dhammapada.meaning: an early collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

notes: The closing verse is paraphrased, not quoted: the outline cites Max Müller's rendering, but his exact wording was not verified. A Keeper may wish to supply Müller's text verbatim.

The Sanskrit verse has one more image than the outline lists (often rendered darkness, or a fault of vision, after the stars), and Kumarajiva's Chinese version gives a different, shorter list; the script follows the outline's images and makes no count. Confirm.
'Explain without taking hold of the explaining, so it's only called explaining' paraphrases the Sanskrit 'as one who would not illuminate; therefore it is called illuminating'; confirm.
Original-language word: taraka as the verse's 'stars'; confirm spelling and pronunciation.
